content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes BinaryQA, 7,800 questions across 1,024 images, collected via image search and expert annotations. The dataset is claimed to be a difficult out-of-distribution testbed for VQA (“versatile”) and has reliable evaluation (yes/no). The paper has both the analysis of the datasets and experiments evaluating 3 models on this dataset in different scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
- Great scoping of the problem for accurate evaluation (similar to BoolQ in the NLP domain: https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044)
- The dataset appears to be qualitatively diverse (but see my comments below)
- A lot of experiments on the model behavior along several dimensions.

## Weaknesses
- Unclear description of dataset construction
- Weak discussion of related work
- Unclear significance. See my comments on diversity, usefulness, and difficulty. Comparison to related work must be better showcased both in terms of clearer writing and experiments to assess the diversity and difficulty of this dataset.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity
My main issue with the clarity is the description of dataset construction and its relation to other datasets (see details below). It would be nice to replace “baseline” models with something more specific. How about adding yes/no only baselines as well?

## Soundness of Dataset construction
My impression is that the dataset construction lacks rigor and justifications. In many cases, there are not enough details for me to judge the soundness of the construction process so as to provide my estimate on the potential utility and biases of the datasets.
1. Skills: The paper claims “Unlike these datasets, questions in our dataset are carefully constructed by experts such that to answer them a detailed inspection of the image is necessary.” However, in Appendix D, it simply provides general statements such as “we generated some phrases and then searched Flicker or Google search to find matching images” and “We then formulated some questions on these images along with answers” → What steps did the authors take/instructions did the authors provide to ensure execution was done right?
2. Question types: I find defining question types based on the terms that appear in them (In Figure 2) quite weird. How did the authors exactly cluster questions?
3. Ambiguity: “In formulating the questions, we tried to remove any ambiguity” → How would the authors define ambiguous questions?
4. Bias: “We did not incorporate any bias towards gender, age, or race during data collection, and tried to be as inclusive as possible in gathering images and formulating questions. We include and balance questions that address different ages and genders.” → How did the authors try to be “as inclusive as possible”? How did the authors balance the questions?
5. Blue rectangle: Based on Appendix D, this is a very small percentage of the questions (17 images). It also distorts the naturalness of the images, so I was wondering if this part is a distraction.

## Significance of the dataset
1. Intrinsic Evaluation, Diversity: Evidence to support the “versatile” trait of the datasets is weak, both in terms of the image domain and question types, relative to relevant datasets. For example, Figure 1 and Appendix A demonstrate the images come from different domains, but only in *a qualitative manner* and *without comparison*. Sampling 100 images from each relevant dataset (such as Open Images-based, Visual Genome-based, Conceptual Captions-based datasets, etc.) and providing a breakdown of image domain types would be much more indicative of the degree of relative diversity.
2. Extrinsic Eval, Usefulness: If I understand correctly, predicting “yes” only would give 62.7% whereas the accuracy of the “baseline” is also 62%. How should we interpret this? Is this baseline too weak? Can the dataset differentiate between “top” models?
3. Extrinsic Eval, Difficulty: How would the authors argue that the dataset is “inherently” more difficult than VQAv2? For example, is this because of (i) the lack of in-domain training data (the baseline, Pythia, and OFA all use VQAv2 training set?), (ii) out-of-domain images, or even (iii) the question length (Section 4.2). 

## Related Work
1. Comparison to other VQA datasets: “Some prominent VQA datasets are listed in Table 1. We describe the relevant ones to our work in the following.” → How are they relevant? In general, Section 2 still needs more work so that we can understand the context better. Can the authors also compare your datasets to the ones on “general” Web images? The following are the datasets that come to mind, some of which were also derived from text queries on popular search engine
- NLVR2: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00491
- WebQA: https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00590
- [On Conceptual Captions] Adversarial VQA: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00245  
- [On Conceptual Captions] MAVERICS-CC3M: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01883
2. Out-of-distribution eval: Since you do not have training sets, it would be nice to discuss in more detail related work on VQA in out-of-distribution settings (below and the ones already included): https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.00377 https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03726 https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.164/, https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12191

## Reproducibility
 The abstract mentions “Data and Code available”.

## Other comments
- Typo: Appendix D: “Flicker” → “Flickr”
content.summary_of_the_review: Currently, the potential utility of the proposed dataset is not convincing as I describe above.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a binary VQA dataset whose answers are either "yes", or "No" and analyze the results of OFA and a simple baseline model on this dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The proposed new test set shows to be more challenging than the proposed methods.

Weakness:
As the VQA task is an open-end problem, the answers can be variable, not just "yes" or "no". Focusing on the binary-formatted questions makes the VQA task to be a variant of image-text matching and reduces its ability to understand the questions of real natural language.  

The paper compares the collected dataset mainly with VQAv2 while considering less about other datasets. For example, GQA is another popular dataset, which also involves phrases to address the relations. VIZWIZ is another existing VQA dataset. Similar to the proposed dataset, it also contains some samples querying about the text. So, what is the difference between your proposed dataset and GQA and VIZWIZ? It would be better to have a more comprehensive comparison of current popular datasets.

As mentioned in the paper, compared with the VQA dataset, the collected data has different data distribution, i.e. length range of questions, and context of the question. Thus, domain shifting could be a reason for the model degradation. It is normal for a model to have performance degradation on an out-of-distribution dataset. I guess a combination of binary queries from the datasets, which excludes the training and corresponding testing set of the testing methods, may also lead to a degradation of testing methods. To support the claim that the dataset is more challenging, a model should be finetuned on a training set collected with the same policies and then test on the proposed test set.

The proposed model interpreting way may have the ability to explore the capabilities of VQA models. While it is not well formulated and extends to the common objects besides the human face. The method can be polished by well defining the processes of the interpreting methods in a general format, (i.e. what to mask? Where to mask? What is the relation between masked regions and investigated image-question pair?). It would be better if the method can be extended to more common objects.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I cannot find much novelty in this paper. 

The proposed dataset is focused on the binary question, which is only a small part of the regular VQA task. 

The author proposed a dataset focus on binary question while not well demonstrating the difference between it and current existing VQA datasets, i.e. GQA, and VIZWIZ.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Generally speaking, I do not think the paper is very novel. The binary questions are common parts of existing VQA datasets. The proposed dataset only compared with VQA while not well demonstrating the difference between it and other VQA datasets. 

Compared with the data collection, a simple choice we can try is to just combine the binary questions from the existing dataset. It is not sure if such a new dataset is really necessary.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new test set for the VQA dataset with Yes/No only questions. The authors claim that this dataset can is of higher quality and more diverse compared to VQA datasets in use today. The paper studies various aspects of the model using the dataset, such as the effect of question lengths, the "yes-bias" of models, etc.  Experiments show that the existing VQA models do poorly on the dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

*[S1]:* Many Desirable Properties: This reviewer agrees that the proposed dataset addresses many of the desiderata for a nice VQA dataset. The images are different enough from the existing dataset (FID score), the questions all have binary answers, they cover a variety of image types, they are 

*[S2]:* The experiments with respect to the models evaluated are thorough and useful: The paper uses both a simple baseline and the latest VQA models for evaluation. I think the choice of models is adequate and provides enough information about how the existing VQA model might fare in this dataset. No complaints there :) 

**Weaknesses**

*[W1]:* Relation to existing work: The paper is severely lacking discussion and comparison to a wide body of literature on dataset bias in VQA and the construction of adversarial datasets that most models find very difficult (VQA-CP, TDIUC, VQA-CE, etc..). Like this paper, even the yes/no questions suffer drastically under these settings. Even when they are cited, they are only mentioned in passing without a discussion about how they relate to the paper's goals of making a generalizable test set.

*[W2]:* Lacking details, small size, and variety: The paper lacks many details about how the dataset was constructed. What are the overarching guiding principles that governed the dataset creation? Who are the annotators? What were their instructions? For human verification, how many questions do all 3 unanimously agree with? What happens to questions that are not unanimous, but that the majority agree with? Is there a relationship between questions with "unanimous" answers and those with a 2-1 split vs. their accuracy by the models?

Furthermore, the dataset is quite small; Are there enough concept coverage to make meaningful conclusions about the broad set of 23 different types of questions? More than half of the categories have less than 200 questions.  The paper also makes much grander claims that are shown (or can be shown) in the paper.  "BinaryVQA questions are supposed to challenge adults." (How?, where are the results supporting this?) and shows that it can challenge VQA models for years to come (This is an indefensible position and should be removed.) 


*[W3]:* It is not clear if the dataset is "difficult" for the right reasons: There are a lot of areas where the difficulty of this dataset seems artificially inflated. Of course, a VQA model not trained to identify synthetically inserted "blue boxes" will do poorly, and indeed it is one of the categories where a more "SoTA" method does worse than the baseline. For many others, it seems like the answers are hard to predict not because they require careful thought but because they are ambiguous (Page 17, Is this a wine opener? GT: Yes, but is it?? ) or maybe even incorrect.  E.g., (Page 18, "Is there a problem with this iron?" GT is yes, but not sure why looks fine to me...??) I know these feel cherry-picked, but I invite the other reviewers, authors, and the AC to look at a bunch of examples. There seem to be a lot of these cases, which are difficult due to being ambiguous, non-standard objects, surreal imagery, and/or other oddities (E.g., an eagle with a banana for a beak, water spout wearing sneakers, an odd clothpin-like object on one side and spoon on the other, a face with multiple pairs of eyes. There are even the famous pillars that look like two faces, and blue/black white/gold dresses in there (Page 19)) Sure, they are difficult, but are they really what we're looking to do with VQA models? Plenty of other works show that spurious correlations and dataset bias pose serious difficulty even for "normal" images and questions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** The paper is clearly written and easy to follow. 

**Quality:** See strengths and weaknesses above. 

**Novelty:** The paper is a fairly useful VQA dataset but there are not a lot of novel concepts in the paper. See strengths and weaknesses above. 

**Reproducibility:** The authors have promised to release the dataset. So, it should be fine.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new dataset for VQA with many desirable properties; However, it also has serious weaknesses in other areas. While it may be curious to see model results on this dataset, I am not sure if it provides any new insights into them compared to existing work.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.details_of_ethics_concerns: I have concerns about age and gender-related questions in the dataset. Some of the questions include questions such as "Is this a woman?", with a "yes/no" answer. This can invite gender-stereotype affirmation and bias towards transgender people. This is not a problem when they appear in question since they are merely a reflection of the question-writers perception of gender E.g., "Is this woman wearing a dress?", but to try to assign an objective answer to "Is this a woman?" based on photographs alone is borderline objectionable.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes binaryVQA, a reduced test set only for the VQA models. The dataset consists of 7800 questions over 1024 images. The paper introduces different types of questions (as mentioned in Table 2), of varying question lengths. The authors find that SOTA VQA models perform poorly over this result.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
 + new dataset for the community (only test set)
Weakness:
 - Unclear why we need this dataset since the limitations of VQA have been well known and new datasets such as CLEVR, SNLI-VE, NLVR have been proposed to address this limitations. 
 - Unclear from paper why the SOTA models perform poorly. Does this require new generalization mechanisms, new types of reasoning or this is just test/train split.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper can explain more clearly in Section 1 why a new dataset or test set is needed. It is also worth comparing this dataset to other datasets that have been proposed that improve for VQA bias and quality. The paper uses OFA model in Abstract etc. and it will be great to explain this early in the paper what is it, how it works and why the results are poor.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a new test set for VQA. From the description of the paper, it appears that the SOTA models perform poorly given the new semantic concepts introduced in BinaryVQA that are not present in VQA. This result is neither surprising nor novel, and I do not recommend accepting this paper.
